                    ### Question
                    A 67-year-old man with stable coronary artery disease comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Aside from occasional exertional chest pain on mowing the lawn or prolonged jogging, he feels well. He goes jogging for 20 minutes once a week and takes a tablet of sublingual nitroglycerine prior to his run to prevent anginal chest pain. The patient would like to run longer distances and asks the physician whether he could increase the dose of the drug prior to running. Administration of higher dosages of this drug is most likely to result in which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Rebound angina
opb. Development of tolerance
opc. Reflex sympathetic activity
opd. Anaphylactic reaction
ope. Coronary artery vasospasm

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Increasing the dose of sublingual nitroglycerine primarily leads to the development of tolerance, as the body adapts to the vasodilatory effects of the drug over time. This is supported by the consensus that frequent use of nitroglycerine can result in diminished effectiveness due to tolerance. While higher doses may also increase the risk of side effects such as hypotension, which could trigger reflex sympathetic activity, the primary concern with chronic use is tolerance development. Anaphylactic reactions are rare and not a common consequence of nitroglycerine use. Therefore, the most likely outcome of increasing the dose of nitroglycerine is the development of tolerance.
